name: breaking bad smile frown

relational_pattern: A small difference in framing reverses the evaluator's expression from pleased to displeased or vice versa.
example_context: A friend likes the phrase 'team lunch' until they hear 'unpaid mandatory team lunch,' so you label the two reactions.
near_miss_context: Both proposals receive the same response and differ only cosmetically; there is no emotional switch to display.

name: Judgmental Volturi
message: Use when a person or group silently judges someone with severe, disapproving scrutiny.
relational_pattern: The target faces a collective look of condemnation rather than an explicit argument.
example_context: You admit to reheating fish in the office microwave, and the entire lunch table responds with this image.
near_miss_context: Friends listen with curiosity and reserve judgment until they know more; the tribunal-like reaction would overstate their response.

name: Smudge the cat
message: Use as a disgusted, offended, or stubbornly rejecting response to an unwanted suggestion or offering.
relational_pattern: The recipient meets what is presented with visible contempt and refusal.
example_context: Someone proposes replacing the good coffee with an instant powder, and you answer with Smudge's appalled stare.
near_miss_context: A friend offers exactly the option you requested and you accept happily; disgust would communicate the opposite.

name: Hydra
message: Use when one conspicuously foolish, weak, or unserious member stands out among otherwise formidable peers.
relational_pattern: A multi-part group contains a comic outlier whose quality falls far below the others.
example_context: Label two polished product features as the fierce heads and the crash-prone settings page as the goofy third head.
near_miss_context: All members of the group are equally competent, so singling one out as the defective head would be arbitrary.

name: slap that button
message: Use when someone accepts, selects, buys, or approves something immediately and with emphatic enthusiasm.
relational_pattern: A desirable option triggers an instant, forceful yes.
example_context: A friend asks whether the group wants an extra day off after the launch, and everyone replies with this button slap.
near_miss_context: The proposal needs careful legal review before any decision; instant approval would misrepresent the hesitation.

name: Whose Line is it Anyway
message: Use when rules, scores, roles, or stated facts are arbitrary, invented, or ultimately irrelevant to the outcome.
relational_pattern: A formal-looking system is exposed as improvised and consequence-free.
example_context: Your office awards points for meeting attendance but never uses them for anything, so the team compares it to this show.
near_miss_context: A tournament's score determines who advances under published rules; the points materially matter.

name: braveheart freedom
message: Use to celebrate breaking free from an oppressive obligation, restriction, dependency, or source of frustration.
relational_pattern: Release from constraint is proclaimed as a dramatic victory for freedom.
example_context: After the team retires a tool everyone hated maintaining, a developer posts this to celebrate liberation from it.
near_miss_context: A person refuses a reasonable safety boundary that protects others; framing that refusal as heroic freedom would distort the issue.

name: Confused Travolta
message: Use when someone looks around for a person, object, explanation, or expected activity that is conspicuously absent.
relational_pattern: Arrival at an empty or unclear scene produces visible, searching confusion.
example_context: You join the scheduled video call on time and find nobody else there, so you send this in the team chat.
near_miss_context: You know exactly where everyone is and are simply waiting for them; the searching confusion would be false.

name: Worst mistake of my life
message: Use immediately after a bad choice backfires, especially when the regret is obvious and the consequences are already chasing you.
relational_pattern: A voluntary decision is followed by instant recognition that it was disastrously wrong.
example_context: Seconds after volunteering to coordinate the reunion, fifty relatives begin sending conflicting requests, and you post this.
near_miss_context: An unavoidable accident happens despite a careful decision; calling it your mistake would assign responsibility inaccurately.

name: Amateurs
message: Use to one-up a displayed mistake, failure, or extreme behavior by revealing an even more spectacular version.
relational_pattern: A supposedly notable example is dismissed as amateur beside the speaker's superior level of chaos or failure.
example_context: A friend says they missed one deadline, and you reply with the time you missed an entire registration window: 'Amateurs.'
near_miss_context: Someone asks a beginner for help learning a skill; belittling them offers no humorous escalation and is needlessly hostile.

name: Guy talking to girl in club
message: Use for an unwanted, one-sided explanation delivered at length to someone who is visibly trapped or uninterested.
relational_pattern: One person enthusiastically lectures while the listener endures the interaction without engagement.
example_context: Caption the speaker as you explaining your fantasy-league strategy and the listener as the friend who only asked what time dinner starts.
near_miss_context: Both friends eagerly trade stories and ask follow-up questions; mutual conversation is not the template's imbalance.

name: I WANT YOU
message: Use as a direct recruitment or call to action aimed at the viewer or a specifically named person.
relational_pattern: An authority figure singles out the audience as the person needed for a mission or responsibility.
example_context: The volunteer group still needs one event photographer, so its organizer posts this with 'I want you to bring a camera.'
near_miss_context: A general announcement provides information without asking anyone to act; the pointed recruitment gesture would add a demand.

name: Trumpet Boy
message: Use when a loud, persistent person or thing keeps intruding on someone who wants to be left alone.
relational_pattern: An oblivious provocateur repeatedly directs noise at an increasingly irritated target.
example_context: Label the trumpet player 'calendar reminders' and the girl 'me trying to enjoy Sunday evening.'
near_miss_context: A friend plays music after everyone enthusiastically asks for it; welcomed entertainment lacks the unwanted provocation.

name: Stop it, Patrick! You're Scaring Him!
message: Use when one person reveals increasingly intense, unsettling, or technical information until another becomes frightened or overwhelmed.
relational_pattern: Escalating disclosure disturbs an audience while a bystander urges the speaker to stop.
example_context: A developer explains each new consequence of the old billing bug to a nervous product manager, and a teammate posts this.
near_miss_context: The explanation reassures the listener and reduces their concern at every step; the fear escalation is absent.

name: Manly Handshake
message: Use to show two people, groups, or concepts bonding over a shared trait, deal, victory, or point of agreement.
relational_pattern: Distinct sides meet in the middle through one strongly shared connection.
example_context: Label the arms 'remote workers' and 'office workers' and the handshake 'muting pointless notifications.'
near_miss_context: The two groups remain opposed on the labeled issue, so a handshake would falsely suggest common ground.

name: jesus watcha doin
message: Use when someone's questionable behavior seems to be observed by a moral authority, conscience, or disapproving presence.
relational_pattern: A private misdeed becomes awkward because judgment appears to be peeking in.
example_context: Your friend admits using the shared streaming password after promising not to, and you respond with Jesus watching from the edge.
near_miss_context: A person openly performs a generous act they have no reason to hide; implied moral suspicion would not fit.

name: Walter White Breaks Down
message: Use for a complete emotional collapse when bad news, loss, guilt, or accumulated pressure finally becomes unbearable.
relational_pattern: Composure gives way to raw distress after the person reaches a breaking point.
example_context: After weeks of revisions, a client asks the team to restore the very first draft, and the designer replies with this breakdown.
near_miss_context: Someone is mildly annoyed by a typo and fixes it in seconds; the scale is far below a genuine collapse.

name: Plane flying from explosions
message: Use when someone escapes, departs, or carries on looking composed while chaos erupts behind them.
relational_pattern: A successful exit is contrasted with the disaster left in its wake.
example_context: A contractor submits the final files and begins vacation just as the client starts a chaotic revision thread, prompting this reaction.
near_miss_context: A colleague stays behind to manage the emergency and accepts responsibility; the carefree getaway framing would misstate their role.

name: Scout opening the fridge
message: Use for repeatedly checking a place despite already knowing that nothing new or useful will be there.
relational_pattern: Habit and faint hope drive another pointless inspection of an unchanged source.
example_context: You refresh an empty inbox five seconds after the last refresh and send this to acknowledge the compulsion.
near_miss_context: A notification confirms that a requested message has arrived; checking now has new information and is not futile repetition.

name: Deep Thoughts
message: Use for mock-philosophical reflection on a question that sounds profound but is often trivial, absurd, or obvious.
relational_pattern: An everyday observation is elevated into exaggerated intellectual contemplation.
example_context: A friend wonders whether a meeting about reducing meetings should count as another meeting and posts this as a deep thought.
near_miss_context: A team is carefully analyzing a difficult ethical decision with real consequences; treating it as faux wisdom could trivialize the work.

name: Omni Man blocks punch
message: Use when an attack, criticism, challenge, or supposed advantage is stopped effortlessly by someone far stronger.
relational_pattern: A threatening move proves powerless against an unbothered superior opponent.
example_context: A competitor boasts that its new feature will crush your product, but it merely copies a capability your team shipped years ago; reply with this block.
near_miss_context: The challenge causes serious damage and forces a desperate recovery, so effortless invulnerability would be inaccurate.

name: Edna Mode No Capes
message: Use to impose an emphatic, categorical ban on a tempting option because its recurring downside is too dangerous or impractical.
relational_pattern: Past failures turn a design preference into a memorable safety rule with no exceptions.
example_context: After another launch fails because of a Friday release, the team adopts 'No Friday deploys!' and posts this.
near_miss_context: A harmless stylistic preference is still under open discussion; invoking a disaster-backed absolute would overstate the evidence.

name: Inception
message: Use when an idea, story, joke, or system contains one layer nested inside another, often recursively.
relational_pattern: A concept repeats within itself or descends through multiple embedded levels.
example_context: Your team schedules a meeting to plan the agenda for another planning meeting, and someone labels it meeting inception.
near_miss_context: Two unrelated tasks happen side by side without one containing the other; mere complexity is not nesting.

name: Why you no
message: Use as a frustrated demand asking why someone will not perform an obvious, desired, or repeatedly requested action.
relational_pattern: A simple unmet expectation is expressed through exaggerated broken-grammar exasperation.
example_context: After the printer rejects the same valid file again, message the office chat with 'Why you no print?'
near_miss_context: You are asking a nuanced question that requires a careful explanation; the rage-comic demand would sound dismissive.

name: Pepe Silvia
message: Use when someone has built an elaborate theory from scattered details and explains the supposed connections with frantic certainty.
relational_pattern: Obsessive investigation turns weak or tangled evidence into a sprawling conspiracy map.
example_context: A coworker links meeting times, coffee orders, and calendar colors to prove a secret reorganization is coming, so the team posts this.
near_miss_context: An auditor presents a short, documented chain of evidence; rigorously supported findings are not conspiracy-board mania.

name: Are you winning son blank template
message: Use for a parent's earnest but slightly awkward attempt to understand or support a child's hobby, game, or online activity.
relational_pattern: Generational distance is bridged by a simple check-in whose wording may miss the activity's real point.
example_context: Your dad texts 'are you winning?' during a long coding competition, and you share this affectionately with your teammates.
near_miss_context: A manager demands performance metrics from an employee; the power dynamic is evaluation, not parental support.

name: Four Naan Jeremy? Four? That's insane
message: Use to express incredulity that someone chose, consumed, bought, or requested an excessive number of one thing.
relational_pattern: A surprisingly large quantity is repeated back as evidence that the person has gone too far.
example_context: A friend orders four desserts for themselves, and the table responds, 'Four? That's insane,' with this format.
near_miss_context: Four batteries are exactly what the device requires; the quantity is functional rather than comically excessive.

name: rick and morty-extra steps
message: Use when a complicated process is revealed to be a familiar simple activity with unnecessary intermediaries.
relational_pattern: Needless procedure disguises an ordinary result as innovation or sophistication.
example_context: A startup describes ordering lunch through three tokens and a chatbot, and your friend observes that it is delivery with extra steps.
near_miss_context: The additional stages provide essential verification and prevent costly errors; they are not decorative complexity.

name: Grim Reaper Claw Machine
message: Use when fate, danger, layoffs, illness, or another grim force appears to be selecting its next target from a group.
relational_pattern: An impersonal threat repeatedly claims members while the survivors wait to see who is chosen next.
example_context: After a bug reaches a different service every day, engineers label the claw 'the incident' and the prizes with team names.
near_miss_context: A transparent rotation assigns routine duties fairly; random ominous victim selection would mischaracterize the process.

name: DBZ FUSION
message: Use when two people, traits, products, or ideas combine to create a hybrid that contains recognizable parts of both.
relational_pattern: Separate identities merge into a single composite with amplified or mixed qualities.
example_context: A friend describes the new café as a library fused with a nightclub, so you label each fighter with one half of the concept.
near_miss_context: One product simply replaces another without retaining any of its features; substitution is not fusion.

name: Metronome
message: Use when someone or something repeatedly swings between two opposite moods, opinions, states, or choices.
relational_pattern: Rapid alternation prevents a stable position from lasting.
example_context: Your group chat changes from 'cancel the trip' to 'book it now' every hour, so you label each side of the metronome.
near_miss_context: A person makes one considered change and then stays consistent; a single transition is not oscillation.

name: What's on your mind?
message: Use to reveal the one thought, obsession, worry, or oddly specific subject occupying someone's mind beneath a calm exterior.
relational_pattern: An outwardly ordinary person is contrasted with the dominant idea inside their head.
example_context: During dinner you keep thinking about whether you locked the office, so you label the skull with that intrusive concern.
near_miss_context: A friend openly tells everyone exactly what they are considering; there is no hidden inner thought to expose.

name: the office bankruptcy
message: Use when someone believes merely declaring a status or outcome will make it legally or practically true.
relational_pattern: A performative announcement is mistaken for the real process needed to produce its result.
example_context: A teammate says 'I declare this project finished' while half the checklist is open, and the group responds with this.
near_miss_context: An authorized official completes the required procedure and then announces the result; the declaration has real force.

name: panic toad
message: Use as a compact visual for sudden panic, alarm, or horrified realization.
relational_pattern: A new fact instantly converts calm into wide-eyed distress.
example_context: You remember at 11:58 p.m. that an assignment is due at midnight and send this to your study group.
near_miss_context: Someone calmly prepares for a known deadline over several days; the abrupt panic reaction would exaggerate their state.

name: Are you two friends?
message: Use when two people give incompatible answers about whether they are friends, exposing a one-sided or awkward relationship.
relational_pattern: One person claims closeness while the other simultaneously denies it.
example_context: Two coworkers are asked whether they are best friends; one says yes and the other says no, so the team recreates this exchange.
near_miss_context: Both people consistently describe the relationship the same way; there is no mismatch for the split answer.

name: Forever alone
message: Use for self-deprecating loneliness, romantic exclusion, or the feeling that everyone else has companionship.
relational_pattern: The speaker casts themself as the solitary outsider to other people's connections.
example_context: Your friends pair off for a couples' quiz and you are the only unpaired guest, so you send this to the chat.
near_miss_context: You intentionally choose a quiet evening alone and feel content; solitude without sadness is not forever-alone despair.

name: One please
message: Use when a shown item, person, experience, or benefit looks so desirable that someone immediately requests one for themself.
relational_pattern: Seeing an appealing example triggers a concise order for the same thing.
example_context: A friend shares a photo of their company-issued nap pod, and you reply 'one please' to express envy.
near_miss_context: You are negotiating the detailed specifications and quantity of a purchase; the minimal reaction cannot communicate those requirements.

name: Finally, inner peace.
message: Use when a long-running irritation, uncertainty, or conflict is finally resolved and calm returns.
relational_pattern: Removal of a persistent disturbance produces satisfying mental quiet.
example_context: After the smoke alarm's low-battery chirp is finally fixed, your household chat posts this in relief.
near_miss_context: The underlying problem remains active and everyone is merely ignoring it; avoidance is not genuine resolution.

name: I am the Senate
message: Use when one person arrogantly claims to embody an institution, group, rule-making body, or all legitimate authority.
relational_pattern: Individual power erases the distinction between the leader and the system meant to constrain them.
example_context: The club president rejects a vote by saying their opinion is the club's opinion, prompting members to post this.
near_miss_context: A spokesperson accurately reports a decision made through the group's normal vote; representation is not monopolized authority.

name: So You Agree
message: Use to seize on someone's admission and show that it supports the conclusion they were resisting.
relational_pattern: A question elicits agreement that exposes a contradiction or concedes the speaker's premise.
example_context: A friend insists meetings are useful but admits they cancel every meeting without an agenda; reply, 'So you agree—agendas matter.'
near_miss_context: The other person explicitly rejects your premise, so claiming agreement would fabricate a concession.

name: Sonic Says
message: Use to deliver a mock public-service lesson, moral, warning, or rule in the style of an educational character segment.
relational_pattern: A simple piece of advice is framed as an authoritative after-school message.
example_context: After a friend loses work by closing an unsaved file, post 'Sonic says: save before you quit.'
near_miss_context: The topic requires nuanced professional guidance with important exceptions; a jokey one-line lesson would oversimplify it.

name: All My Homies Love
message: Use to show that an entire friend group enthusiastically approves of, supports, or enjoys the same person or thing.
relational_pattern: Collective loyalty turns a preference into a shared group identity.
example_context: Your friends unanimously praise the colleague who always brings snacks, so you caption the group 'All my homies love Maya.'
near_miss_context: The group is split and several members dislike the subject; claiming universal affection would erase the disagreement.

name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
message: Use to rank needs or desires from foundational priorities to an exaggerated, highly specific ultimate aspiration.
relational_pattern: A familiar hierarchy is repurposed to show what supposedly matters more at each ascending level.
example_context: A student labels the pyramid from sleep and food at the base to 'professor cancels the exam' at the peak.
near_miss_context: The items have no dependency or increasing importance and are simply listed alphabetically; a hierarchy would imply structure that is absent.

name: worship the lord
message: Use when someone treats a person, object, brand, or idea with absurdly reverent devotion.
relational_pattern: Ordinary admiration is elevated into ceremonial worship of a supposed supreme figure.
example_context: When the office's temperamental printer finally produces a perfect color proof, the designers jokingly bow to it with this image.
near_miss_context: A person is sincerely discussing their religious practice; using an ironic worship template may be disrespectful and unclear.

name: My precious Gollum
message: Use for jealous, possessive attachment to something a person treasures and refuses to share or surrender.
relational_pattern: Value becomes obsession, turning the owner defensive toward anyone who approaches the prized object.
example_context: Your sibling asks to borrow the last piece of cake you saved, and you clutch the container while replying 'my precious.'
near_miss_context: You happily offer an item to anyone who needs it; generosity is the opposite of Gollum-like possession.

name: oh thats a toilet spongebob fish
message: Use when someone belatedly recognizes an obvious object's identity or purpose after treating it in a misguided way.
relational_pattern: A mundane realization arrives only after the person has already made an embarrassing mistake.
example_context: A coworker spends five minutes searching for the mute control before realizing the large microphone icon is the button, prompting this response.
near_miss_context: A specialist correctly identifies unfamiliar equipment before touching it; there is no late, humiliating discovery.

name: I WANT PICTURES OF SPIDERMAN
message: Use for a boss, editor, fan, or stakeholder repeatedly demanding one very specific kind of content or deliverable.
relational_pattern: An obsessive requester reduces every priority to obtaining the same desired material.
example_context: The marketing lead ignores every campaign update and asks only for fresh customer photos, so the team paraphrases the demand with this.
near_miss_context: A client makes a single flexible request and welcomes alternatives; that lacks the recurring fixation on one output.

name: Impressive, very nice
message: Use for praise that is outwardly controlled but loaded with envy, rivalry, status comparison, or barely concealed insecurity.
relational_pattern: A polished compliment masks the speaker's discomfort at being outclassed.
example_context: A colleague shows an exceptionally elegant portfolio, and you jokingly reply 'Impressive, very nice' while comparing it to your own.
near_miss_context: You warmly congratulate a friend with no competitive subtext; a jealous appraisal would add an unintended edge.

name: here's johnny
message: Use for a sudden, forceful, or uninvited entrance that startles people already inside a conversation or space.
relational_pattern: An intruder announces their arrival by breaking through an expected boundary.
example_context: A coworker unexpectedly appears in a quiet thread with the answer everyone was avoiding, and posts 'Here's Johnny.'
near_miss_context: A host introduces the scheduled speaker at the agreed time; a normal entrance lacks the intrusive surprise.

name: Dafuq did I just read
message: Use after reading something so incoherent, bizarre, offensive, or mentally taxing that ordinary confusion is insufficient.
relational_pattern: Written material provokes stunned disbelief about what the reader has just encountered.
example_context: A friend forwards a paragraph whose argument contradicts itself in every sentence, and you respond with this reaction.
near_miss_context: The document is clear but you disagree with its conclusion; disagreement alone is not bewilderment at the text itself.

name: HOMER BUSH
message: Use when someone quietly retreats from an awkward, embarrassing, contentious, or unwanted situation.
relational_pattern: A person reverses out of view rather than remain associated with what is happening.
example_context: You enter a chat just as two relatives begin arguing about politics, so you post Homer backing into the hedge and leave.
near_miss_context: A teammate stays to mediate the conflict openly; they are engaging rather than disappearing.

name: gondor calls for aid
message: Use when one group urgently asks an ally for help and the relationship implies that the ally will answer.
relational_pattern: A prior bond or mutual duty turns a distress call into expected reciprocal support.
example_context: The support team is overwhelmed during launch and calls engineering for aid; engineering replies that it will answer.
near_miss_context: A stranger demands unpaid work from someone with no relationship or obligation to them; reciprocity is missing.

name: Nobody Expects the Spanish Inquisition Monty Python
message: Use when an unexpected person, event, demand, or complication abruptly interrupts an otherwise ordinary situation.
relational_pattern: Surprise itself is the joke: the audience could not reasonably anticipate the intervention.
example_context: A routine status meeting is suddenly joined by the chief executive, and someone messages that nobody expected the inquisition.
near_miss_context: The agenda clearly announced the guest weeks ago; calling the arrival unexpected would ignore shared notice.

name: Forest Gump Running
message: Use when someone keeps going far beyond the expected stopping point, or abruptly decides to run away from the situation altogether.
relational_pattern: Movement becomes an extended commitment whose distance or duration surprises observers.
example_context: A friend begins a short cleanup and reorganizes the entire apartment overnight, so the group compares their momentum to Forrest running.
near_miss_context: Someone completes precisely the small errand they planned and stops; ordinary follow-through lacks the runaway scale.

name: Captain america elevator
message: Use when people sharing a confined setting realize a confrontation is imminent and tension spikes before anyone acts.
relational_pattern: Close physical proximity turns an unspoken conflict into an unavoidable showdown.
example_context: Two colleagues who publicly criticized each other step into the same elevator before a meeting, and the office chat posts this.
near_miss_context: The passengers are relaxed strangers making small talk; an impending fight would invent tension that is not there.

name: This Little Manuever is Gonna Cost us 51 Years
message: Use when a clever-looking action, shortcut, or tradeoff succeeds only by imposing a comically enormous long-term cost.
relational_pattern: Immediate progress is purchased with disproportionate delay or damage later.
example_context: The team skips a one-day migration and thereby commits to maintaining the old system for years, prompting this line.
near_miss_context: A maneuver saves time now without creating future debt; there is no delayed price to exaggerate.

name: Hans Landa hiding enemies of the state
message: Use for a tense interrogation in which someone must conceal a secret, protect another person, or survive an authority figure's probing questions.
relational_pattern: Hidden information sits dangerously close to a skilled questioner who suspects more than is being said.
example_context: A manager asks who organized the unauthorized farewell party while the organizer sits silently beside you, and you share this scene afterward.
near_miss_context: A friend asks a casual question and everyone is free to answer honestly; there is no concealed target or coercive scrutiny.

name: Professor Farnsworth Good News Everyone
message: Use to announce news with upbeat confidence when the information is dubious, inconvenient, or likely to be bad for the audience.
relational_pattern: Cheerful framing clashes with the unwelcome substance of the announcement.
example_context: The project lead says, 'Good news, everyone—we get another weekend to redo the migration,' and posts this.
near_miss_context: You are sharing genuinely welcome news with no catch or irony; the ominous cheerfulness may imply a hidden downside.

name: spongebob wanna see me do it again
message: Use when someone performs an impressive, reckless, annoying, or absurd feat and immediately offers to repeat it.
relational_pattern: A completed action becomes a boast through effortless, eager repetition.
example_context: After finding one bug in seconds, a tester finds another identical one and asks the developers, 'Wanna see me do it again?'
near_miss_context: A person fails once and is reluctant to retry; the template requires confidence and repeatability rather than hesitant recovery.

name: Straining kid
message: Use when a simple task, decision, or act of self-control requires visibly disproportionate effort.
relational_pattern: Minor resistance is portrayed as an exhausting full-body struggle.
example_context: You try not to correct a harmless typo in a casual group chat and send this to show the effort of staying silent.
near_miss_context: A genuinely strenuous emergency rescue demands major exertion; the humor depends on effort being excessive for the task.

name: Squidward competition
message: Use when entering a competition only to discover that the opponent is uniquely dominant at the exact skill being tested.
relational_pattern: Hope collapses because the matchup favors an unbeatable specialist.
example_context: You enter a trivia round about your coworker's hometown and learn that coworker is your opponent, so you post this.
near_miss_context: The opponent is inexperienced and the contest is evenly matched; doomed recognition would be premature.

name: "We did it, Patrick! We saved the City!"
message: Use to celebrate a supposed success when the attempted solution has actually caused enormous damage or made the problem worse.
relational_pattern: Self-congratulation ignores the destruction produced by the 'rescue.'
example_context: After removing one spam post by accidentally deleting the entire forum, an admin jokes, 'We did it—we saved the community.'
near_miss_context: A careful fix solves the problem without collateral harm; ironic failure-celebration would be undeserved.

name: Dodge chad vs virgin
message: Use to contrast an admired, powerful, or confident version of something with a weaker, awkward, or inferior counterpart.
relational_pattern: Two archetypes are exaggerated into a dominant ideal and a pitiable alternative.
example_context: Compare the colleague who documents a fix for everyone with the colleague who silently patches production and tells nobody.
near_miss_context: The two choices have balanced strengths and neither is clearly framed as superior; the caricature would force a false hierarchy.

name: I'm awake, but at what cost?
message: Use when achieving wakefulness required so little sleep or such unpleasant effort that being awake feels like a bad bargain.
relational_pattern: The desired state is reached, but exhaustion makes its cost dominate the result.
example_context: After three coffees get you through an early meeting following two hours of sleep, send this to your team.
near_miss_context: You wake naturally after a full night's rest and feel refreshed; there is no painful tradeoff.

name: Borat i go to america
message: Use when announcing a trip, move, or visit with conspicuous excitement and slightly naive confidence.
relational_pattern: Eager arrival: an outsider enthusiastically sets off for an unfamiliar destination and imagines the adventure ahead.
example_context: A friend gets approval for their first international conference and posts 'I go to Berlin' before booking anything else.
near_miss_context: Avoid for an ordinary commute to a familiar office; the format needs novelty, travel, and outsized anticipation.

name: Gunna Writes In Fire Meme
message: Use to praise writing, music, an argument, or creative work as exceptionally good—as though the creator is producing fire.
relational_pattern: High-quality output turns the ordinary act of making it into a visibly blazing performance.
example_context: A friend delivers a devastatingly funny comeback in the group chat, and you reply that they are writing in fire.
near_miss_context: The message is careless and unconvincing; using the template sincerely would praise work you mean to criticize.

name: Smash Bros.
message: Use to announce that a new participant, faction, idea, or complication has dramatically entered an ongoing conflict.
relational_pattern: An existing contest changes when another combatant joins the field.
example_context: Two departments debate a policy until legal adds a third position, and the chat announces that legal joins the battle.
near_miss_context: One side quietly leaves and nobody new enters; the battlefield has shrunk rather than gained a participant.

name: Mean Girls - Stop Trying to Make Fetch Happen
message: Use to tell someone to stop forcing a phrase, trend, plan, nickname, or idea that plainly is not catching on.
relational_pattern: Repeated promotion cannot manufacture the social acceptance the advocate wants.
example_context: A coworker uses the same awkward project nickname in every meeting despite nobody adopting it, so the team sends this.
near_miss_context: A new term has spread organically and everyone already uses it; declaring it impossible would lag behind reality.

name: Change My Mind (tilt-corrected)
message: Use to state a debatable opinion with conspicuous confidence and invite others to challenge it.
relational_pattern: A provocative claim is presented as the starting position for public argument, not as a surrendered belief.
example_context: Post 'Breakfast food is better at dinner—change my mind' to start a playful debate among friends.
near_miss_context: You have already reconsidered after new evidence and want to announce your updated view; the template instead signals current conviction.

name: Show me the money
message: Use when someone demands concrete payment, revenue, funding, or financial proof instead of promises and enthusiasm.
relational_pattern: Commitment is made conditional on seeing real money rather than projections or praise.
example_context: A client offers exposure instead of a fee, and the freelancer replies with this to insist on actual compensation.
near_miss_context: A volunteer explicitly agreed to an unpaid community role; introducing a payment ultimatum changes the arrangement.

name: Kramer, what's going on in there
message: Use when alarming, bizarre, or chaotic activity is clearly happening nearby but remains hidden from view.
relational_pattern: An observer confronts someone at the boundary of a concealed disturbance and demands an explanation.
example_context: Your neighbors' renovation produces a crash followed by cheering, so you message a friend with this reaction.

example_context: Your usually punctual friend arrives five minutes late, and the group mock-announces the event in giant newspaper type.
near_miss_context: You are quietly sharing sensitive information with one trusted person; headline treatment would violate the intended privacy.

name: Ain't Nobody Got Time For That
message: Use when rejecting a tedious, unnecessary, or time-consuming demand
relational_pattern: You decline a request that wastes your time
example_context: Someone proposes a daily two-hour status call, and the team answers that nobody has time for it.
near_miss_context: The task is brief, necessary, and prevents a larger failure; inconvenience alone does not make it pointless.

name: Steve Harvey Laughing Serious
message: Use when laughter stops instantly after a new detail makes the subject serious, personal, or threatening.
relational_pattern: Amusement flips to concern once the joke's hidden implication lands.
example_context: You laugh at a story about forgotten anniversaries until your partner asks today's date, then send this two-stage reaction.
near_miss_context: The conversation stays light and everyone keeps laughing; there is no sobering turn for the second panel.

name: The Rock Explaining
message: Use when earnestly explaining an obvious point at excessive length
relational_pattern: You over-explain a simple concept with unnecessary detail
example_context: You ask where lunch is, and your colleague begins explaining the history of urban zoning; send this overexplanation reaction.
near_miss_context: The listener requested the background and needs it to decide; detail can be relevant rather than excessive.

name: Sofa explosion
message: Use when a calm or comfortable situation is abruptly destroyed by a wildly disruptive event.
relational_pattern: Normality holds for one beat before chaos erupts without warning.
example_context: A quiet family chat suddenly receives fifty messages about an old inheritance dispute, and you compare it to the exploding sofa.
near_miss_context: A planned announcement arrives on schedule and everyone responds calmly; expected change is not a surprise detonation.

name: Now that's a name I haven't heard since...
message: Use when hearing an old name or topic that revives distant memories
relational_pattern: An old reference triggers nostalgic recollections
example_context: A friend mentions an abandoned app everyone used in college, and you answer with the old-name line.
near_miss_context: The subject was discussed yesterday and remains active; the reference is not distant enough to awaken nostalgia.

name: Baby Boss Relaxed Smug Content
message: Use when relaxed smugness follows getting exactly what was wanted
relational_pattern: You feel content after achieving a desired outcome
example_context: Your proposal is approved exactly as written, so you post the relaxed Boss Baby while everyone else debates revisions.
near_miss_context: You are still waiting anxiously for a decision; smug contentment would claim an outcome that has not arrived.

name: I am the danger
message: Use when rejecting the role of victim and claiming to be the real threat
relational_pattern: You assert yourself as the source of danger rather than the target
example_context: A competitor warns that your teammate may be outmatched, and the teammate replies that they are the danger.
near_miss_context: You face a credible threat and are asking others for protection; dominance would be empty bravado.

name: Why would X do this
message: Use when someone causes a problem and then hypocritically blames an innocent person, group, or force for it.
relational_pattern: The perpetrator poses as a confused victim of their own deliberate action.
example_context: A manager cancels testing, ships a broken release, and asks why quality assurance allowed it; the team uses this format privately.
near_miss_context: An investigator traces a failure to its actual external cause; accurate attribution is not self-exonerating blame.

name: Girls whispering
message: Use when sharing private gossip or side commentary about someone nearby
relational_pattern: You discuss someone's private matters in a low voice
example_context: Two friends quietly exchange reactions while the person they are discussing gives a speech nearby; use this for the side commentary.
near_miss_context: The comment is addressed openly to the person and everyone can hear it; secrecy is essential to the whispering setup.

name: magic 8 ball
message: Use when handing an uncertain prediction or decision over to arbitrary, pseudo-mystical chance.
relational_pattern: A yes-or-no question receives random guidance instead of evidence-based judgment.
example_context: Nobody knows whether the client will reply today, so a teammate jokingly asks the Magic 8 Ball.
near_miss_context: The team has reliable data and a defined decision rule; pretending the answer is random would ignore usable evidence.

name: Spongebob - "I Don't Need It" (by Henry-C)
message: Use when trying to resist a temptation while desire visibly intensifies
relational_pattern: You struggle against a growing urge to act
example_context: You keep refusing dessert until someone opens the box beside you, then post the panels as your resolve collapses.
near_miss_context: The offer holds no appeal and declining it is effortless; desire must intensify for the progression to work.

name: I am speed
message: Use when psyching yourself up to act exceptionally fast, often with more confidence than the task warrants.
relational_pattern: A declaration of speed precedes a rushed attempt or quick turnaround.
example_context: You have five minutes to clean before guests arrive and post 'I am speed' before starting.
near_miss_context: The work requires slow verification and you intentionally proceed carefully; speed is not the goal.

name: Arrested Development how much would a banana cost
message: Use when someone reveals wealth or privilege by wildly overestimating the price of an ordinary item.
relational_pattern: Distance from everyday costs produces a confidently absurd guess.
example_context: An executive estimates that a bus ticket costs fifty dollars, and employees respond with the banana quote.
near_miss_context: A shopper checks a fluctuating price because they are budgeting carefully; uncertainty is not privileged detachment.

name: Being/working as xxxxxx is not stressful at all
message: Use when someone insists a role or situation is not stressful while their appearance or surroundings prove the opposite.
relational_pattern: Verbal denial clashes with visible evidence of severe strain.
example_context: The event organizer says planning is relaxing while answering three phones and fixing a leak, so the team posts this.
near_miss_context: Someone reports low stress and is visibly calm with a manageable workload; the contradiction required by the meme is absent.

name: 2/3 wolves laugh
message: Use when two members share a joke while a third is excluded or unimpressed
relational_pattern: Two people laugh together while ignoring a third person
example_context: Two teammates laugh at an inside joke while the new colleague stares blankly, so you label the three wolves.
near_miss_context: All three people understand and enjoy the joke together; nobody occupies the excluded or unimpressed role.

name: Dinkleberg Blank
message: Use when using one familiar scapegoat for every unrelated inconvenience
relational_pattern: You blame a common figure for unrelated issues
example_context: The Wi-Fi fails, it rains, and you lose a sock; blame the same rival for all three with a resentful 'Dinkleberg.'
near_miss_context: Evidence connects a specific person to the one problem being discussed; accurate responsibility is not scapegoating.

name: clown computer
message: Use when someone's online post, search, purchase, or argument makes them look foolish by their own hand.
relational_pattern: Digital activity becomes a self-administered clown costume.
example_context: A friend argues with an obvious parody account for an hour, and the group sends this computer-clown reaction.
near_miss_context: A person is deceived by a sophisticated fraud despite reasonable caution; ridicule would unfairly blame the victim.

name: Drunk Guy Talking To Girl
message: Use when someone delivers a long, passionate monologue to a listener who is visibly disengaged or trapped.
relational_pattern: The speaker's intensity grows while the audience offers no reciprocal interest.
example_context: At a party you explain your keyboard layout for twenty minutes to someone scanning the room for an exit; post this afterward.
near_miss_context: Both people ask questions and enthusiastically trade detailed stories; mutual engagement is not a one-sided ramble.

name: Grandpa Simpson Hat
message: Use when someone arrives, immediately recognizes an unwanted situation, and leaves without engaging.
relational_pattern: Entry and exit collapse into one quick reversal after a single glance.
example_context: You join a call, hear that it is an icebreaker session, and disconnect before anyone notices; send this in the private chat.
near_miss_context: A participant stays to address the problem despite initial discomfort; they did not perform the instant turnaround.

name: Homelander applause
message: Use when receiving approval that feels forced, performative, or unsettling
relational_pattern: The approval is generated by external pressure rather than genuine acceptance
example_context: The boss finishes a threatening speech and everyone claps because nobody wants to be first to stop; post this unsettling applause.
near_miss_context: Colleagues spontaneously celebrate a well-earned achievement; genuine warmth lacks the coercive undertone.

name: Fortune Cookie
message: Use to package a prediction, tiny piece of advice, or suspiciously convenient claim as mock fortune-cookie wisdom.
relational_pattern: Authority through packaging: an ordinary opinion is presented as if fate delivered a concise prophecy.
example_context: A friend predicts the delayed bus will arrive the moment everyone orders a taxi, so you frame the guess as today's fortune.
near_miss_context: Avoid when quoting verified guidance from a qualified source; the joke depends on flimsy prophecy or bite-sized pseudo-wisdom.

name: Angry pingu
message: Use when small frustrations escalate into disproportionate fury
relational_pattern: Minor annoyances trigger an exaggerated emotional response that exceeds the initial problem's significance
example_context: The printer jams once during a quiet afternoon and your friend reacts as if personally betrayed, so you send Angry Pingu.
near_miss_context: A repeated failure has serious consequences and the person voices proportionate concern; not all anger is comic excess.

name: Soldiers hold up society
message: Use to show that overlooked workers, systems, or institutions carry the burden that lets everyone else function normally.
relational_pattern: Visible society rests on a small, strained support layer receiving little recognition.
example_context: During a smooth launch, someone credits the two operations engineers quietly keeping every service alive with this image.
near_miss_context: A celebrated leader receives ample support while contributing little infrastructure; placing them underneath society would invert the burden.

name: For Christmas I Want a Dragon
message: Use when an impossible wish is treated as easier to grant than a supposedly realistic but extraordinarily unlikely request.
relational_pattern: The fallback to fantasy exposes how hopeless the original demand sounds.
example_context: A friend asks for a cheap apartment beside the office, and you reply, 'What color dragon would you like?'
near_miss_context: The practical request is readily available within budget; replacing it with fantasy would not reveal impossibility.

name: thank you for changing my life
message: Use to give dramatically oversized gratitude for a small tip, convenience, recommendation, or kindness.
relational_pattern: A modest benefit is celebrated as a life-altering intervention.
example_context: A coworker shows you a keyboard shortcut that saves two clicks, and you respond, 'Thank you for changing my life.'
near_miss_context: Someone provides life-saving aid during an emergency; sincere major gratitude should not be reduced to a tiny-favor joke.

name: Not stonks
message: Use when a decision or outcome is plainly financially or strategically bad
relational_pattern: The result of a choice has clear negative consequences that are obvious to the decision-maker
example_context: You pay rush shipping that costs more than the item, and the group replies 'not stonks.'
near_miss_context: A costly choice buys a clearly valued benefit after informed comparison; expense alone is not strategic failure.

name: Who the f**k starts a conversation like that I just sat down!
message: Use when someone's opening line is so intense, intimate, hostile, or bizarre that it overwhelms the conversation before it begins.
relational_pattern: A listener who has barely arrived is confronted with an inappropriately extreme first remark.
example_context: You join lunch and a friend immediately asks which family member you would rescue first; answer with this line.
near_miss_context: The conversation develops naturally before reaching a difficult subject; the shock depends on the remark coming first.

name: yo dawg i heard you like
message: Use when nesting a thing inside another version of itself so someone can experience it while experiencing it.
relational_pattern: Recursive duplication turns a preference into an absurd layered construction.
example_context: A coworker embeds a dashboard inside a dashboard and says it lets you monitor dashboards while monitoring dashboards.
near_miss_context: You merely recommend a second unrelated item someone may enjoy; parallel suggestions are not recursive nesting.

name: So anyway I started blasting
message: Use when someone skips deliberation and responds to a problem with immediate, excessive, chaotic action.
relational_pattern: A brief setup jumps straight to an overreaction with no measured intermediate step.
example_context: Asked how they handled one spam email, your friend says they blocked the entire company domain: 'Anyway, I started blasting.'
near_miss_context: A team investigates carefully and applies the smallest effective fix; restraint is the opposite of blasting.

name: Thor is he though
message: Use when challenging a confident claim with dry skepticism
relational_pattern: The response questions the validity of a statement through understated doubt
example_context: Someone declares the new hire a genius before their first day, and you answer with Thor's skeptical 'Is he though?'
near_miss_context: The claim is supported by clear evidence and you have no reason to doubt it; reflexive skepticism adds nothing.

name: Tell me the truth, I'm ready to hear it
message: Use when bracing for an unpleasant fact and asking for blunt honesty
relational_pattern: The request for truth is made in anticipation of negative information
example_context: Before opening the review comments, you ask your teammate to tell you plainly how bad they are.
near_miss_context: You are fishing for reassurance and reject every honest answer; the format claims readiness to accept an unpleasant truth.

name: Quit Having Fun
message: Use to mock a scold who condemns other people's harmless enjoyment because it is unfashionable, unserious, or not to their taste.
relational_pattern: Personal dislike is presented as a moral rule that everyone else must stop having fun.
example_context: Someone writes an essay about why adults should not enjoy a silly game, and fans answer with this comic.
near_miss_context: An activity is harming participants or bystanders; criticism based on real consequences is not joyless gatekeeping.

name: Dr Manhattan explosive arguments
message: Use when someone deploys overwhelming force, knowledge, or rhetorical complexity to obliterate a minor argument.
relational_pattern: A trivial disagreement receives a response so powerful that it becomes comic overkill.
example_context: A friend disputes one date, and you answer with a sourced twenty-page timeline; the group compares it to Dr. Manhattan.
near_miss_context: You offer one concise fact that resolves a consequential dispute; proportionate evidence is not explosive overkill.

name: Table Flip Guy
message: Use when an abrupt burst of frustration ends the discussion
relational_pattern: The frustration causes a sudden termination of communication
example_context: After the spreadsheet corrupts for the third time, you post the table flip and abandon the discussion for the evening.
near_miss_context: A disagreement ends through calm compromise; explosive frustration would misstate the resolution.

name: Spongebob yeet
message: Use when discarding an unwanted object, idea, or responsibility without hesitation
relational_pattern: The action of discarding is immediate and without consideration
example_context: A proposed feature creates five security problems, so the reviewer immediately yeets it out of the roadmap.
near_miss_context: The idea remains useful and is being set aside temporarily for research; instant disposal implies final rejection.

name: You have no power here
message: Use when someone's threat, title, rule, or usual authority has no force in the present setting.
relational_pattern: A would-be controller discovers that their power ends at a jurisdictional boundary.
example_context: The office organizer tries to enforce the dress code in a weekend gaming chat, and members answer with this.
near_miss_context: The person is responsible for the venue and is applying a valid safety rule; their authority plainly does apply.

name: Computer Guy Facepalm
message: Use when reacting to an obvious digital mistake with exhausted embarrassment
relational_pattern: The reaction is a mix of embarrassment and frustration over a simple error
example_context: A developer discovers the outage came from their own missing comma and sends this exhausted facepalm to the incident channel.
near_miss_context: The failure came from an obscure provider defect nobody could reasonably predict; personal embarrassment is misplaced.

name: Dos Equis Guy Awesome
message: Use in the 'I don't always X, but when I do, Y' structure to describe an infrequent behavior with a witty, confident payoff.
relational_pattern: A rare action is paired with the speaker's characteristic way of doing it.
example_context: Write, 'I don't always reply-all, but when I do, it is to the entire company,' after an email mistake.
near_miss_context: The behavior happens constantly and the second clause adds no distinctive outcome; the format depends on rarity plus payoff.

name: Sure Jan
message: Use to answer an implausible excuse, boast, or denial with polite-looking but unmistakable disbelief.
relational_pattern: Surface agreement carries a sarcastic refusal to accept the claim.
example_context: A friend says their five-hour late arrival was caused by one red light, and you reply, 'Sure, Jan.'
near_miss_context: A trusted person provides a well-supported explanation and you genuinely accept it; sarcasm would falsely accuse them of lying.

name: simpsons alguien quiere pensar en los niños
message: Use when someone invokes 'the children' to add melodramatic moral panic to an otherwise minor dispute.
relational_pattern: An emotional appeal substitutes imagined danger to children for proportionate evidence.
example_context: During a debate about changing the office snack shelf, someone jokingly cries, 'Won't somebody please think of the children?'
near_miss_context: A policy presents a documented, immediate risk to children; raising their safety is substantive rather than theatrical panic.

name: Satisfaction
message: Use when enjoying the relief of a result fitting perfectly
relational_pattern: The response indicates satisfaction from a perfectly aligned outcome
example_context: A misaligned button finally snaps into the exact grid position, and the designer shares this deeply satisfied reaction.
near_miss_context: The result merely passes while visible defects remain; adequacy is not the perfect fit the meme celebrates.

name: Could you not ___ for 5 MINUTES
message: Use to beg someone or something to pause one relentless, irritating behavior for even a very short time.
relational_pattern: Accumulated frustration reduces the request to five minutes of relief.
example_context: The group chat has turned every topic into the same argument all day, so you ask whether it can not do that for five minutes.
near_miss_context: The behavior occurred once and stopped immediately after a polite request; there is no relentless pattern behind the exasperation.

name: may i please get a crumb
message: Use when humbly pleading for a tiny share of attention, money, access, credit, or another resource controlled by someone with plenty.
relational_pattern: A powerless requester asks for the smallest concession from visible abundance.
example_context: After executives announce record profits, an employee posts this while asking whether raises will exceed one percent.
near_miss_context: Two peers negotiate an equal division and both have real leverage; the crumb format implies extreme imbalance.

name: Trying to calculate how much sleep I can get
message: Use when doing late-night arithmetic to justify staying awake a little longer
relational_pattern: The action involves calculating sleep time to rationalize extended wakefulness
example_context: At 1 a.m. you recalculate how many hours remain if you watch one more episode and send this equation-filled reaction.
near_miss_context: You set a fixed bedtime and stop negotiating with yourself; there is no late-night rationalization.

name: Lorax Money
message: Use when someone abandons environmental, ethical, or stated values as soon as profit becomes available.
relational_pattern: Principles disappear at the moment money offers a stronger incentive.
example_context: A brand drops its no-ads promise after one lucrative sponsorship offer, and users respond with the money-focused Lorax.
near_miss_context: A company rejects profitable work because it violates its published standards; the choice preserves rather than sells out its values.

name: Keep my wifes name out of your mouth
message: Use as an explosive warning to stop insulting, mocking, or repeatedly mentioning someone the speaker fiercely defends.
relational_pattern: A public joke about a loved person crosses a boundary and triggers immediate confrontation.
example_context: Friends keep teasing your teammate after being asked to stop, and you quote the line as an exaggerated defense.
near_miss_context: Someone offers respectful, requested feedback about a public decision; treating critique as a personal attack would be disproportionate.

name: pouring gas on fire
message: Use when making an already bad conflict or failure substantially worse
relational_pattern: The action intensifies an existing negative situation through additional harm
example_context: Two teammates are already arguing, and a third forwards an insulting old message into the thread; label that intervention as gasoline.
near_miss_context: A mediator lowers the temperature and clarifies the misunderstanding; productive de-escalation does not feed the fire.

name: Do You Wanna Build A Snowman
message: Use when repeatedly inviting an unresponsive person to join an activity
relational_pattern: The invitation persists despite lack of engagement from the recipient
example_context: You keep inviting a withdrawn friend to the weekly game, leaving gentle messages even when they do not answer.
near_miss_context: The person has clearly asked for space and further contact would violate that boundary; persistence is not always affectionate.

name: one of us
message: Use when welcoming or pressuring a newcomer into the group's shared identity
relational_pattern: The statement creates a sense of belonging through group identity
example_context: A new coworker begins using the team's obscure shorthand, and everyone chants 'one of us' to welcome them.
near_miss_context: The newcomer is pressured to abandon an important boundary to fit in; coercive conformity is not harmless belonging.

name: PlayStation trophy
message: Use when treating a small everyday accomplishment like an unlocked achievement
relational_pattern: The accomplishment is framed as a significant milestone in a gaming context
example_context: You finally empty the laundry basket and jokingly announce that you unlocked the 'Floor Visible' trophy.
near_miss_context: The achievement required years of work and carries formal recognition; reducing it to a trivial unlock may understate it.

name: Patrick Star and Man Ray
message: Use when patient step-by-step logic makes someone accept every premise, yet they still reject the unavoidable conclusion.
relational_pattern: Reasoning succeeds locally but fails at the final inference because the other person refuses consistency.
example_context: A coworker agrees the task is done, agrees done tasks leave the board, then insists it must stay; share the wallet exchange.
near_miss_context: New evidence legitimately breaks the chain between the premises and conclusion; revising the answer is not irrational refusal.

name: Is mayonnaise an instrument?
message: Use for an earnest question that is hilariously off-topic or makes an obvious category error.
relational_pattern: Confident participation produces a query showing that the speaker misunderstood the entire subject.
example_context: During a discussion of programming languages, someone asks whether Excel counts as a database, and the group uses this reaction.
near_miss_context: A beginner asks a relevant foundational question whose answer is not obvious; curiosity alone should not be mocked.

name: Random Bullshit Go
message: Use when someone throws many unrelated tools, claims, tactics, or ideas at a problem without a coherent plan.
relational_pattern: Quantity and improvisation replace strategy in a frantic barrage.
example_context: With the demo failing, a teammate restarts three services, changes the Wi-Fi, clears caches, and says 'random bullshit, go.'
near_miss_context: A responder follows a tested diagnostic sequence where each step narrows the cause; variety alone is not randomness.

name: It never was
message: Use to reveal that a supposed distinction, assumption, or prior state was false from the very beginning.
relational_pattern: A surprised question receives the correction that the truth has always been otherwise.
example_context: Someone asks, 'Wait, this meeting was just another sales pitch?' and you answer, 'It always was.'
near_miss_context: The situation genuinely changed recently from one state to another; claiming it was always that way erases the transition.
